chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
title: W. C. Handy's royalties and the dedication of his cabin
summary: She recounts a Cleveland Press article on Handy's lack of royalties and attending the dedication of his Florence cabin in cold weather.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Where the blues came from: Handy, Bolden and early blues

blocks.x: Okay, we've been talking off tape a little bit about some of the items you have in your collection. We've been looking at sheet of music for the "St. Louis Blues" which W.C. Handy autographed for you.

Personally. And that reminds me of something you said way back at the very beginning of the interviewing. You said that W. C. Handy didn't collect any royalties, and I wasn't sure about that at the time. I looked up in his autobiography and I could find only the statement that's for "Memphis Blues" he didn't because he sold it outright for $50. But when it came to the "St Louis Blues" he was involved in some kind of a publishing venture which gave him some return on it.

Yeah, well from what I can understand, that up until the time when this picture was made that he was not receiving royalties on "St. Louis Blues". Of course, on the back of this sheet of music there's an article in here about the American Composer's Society. ---ASCAP.

S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC.
WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
Where is the article from and what's the date?

This article is from the Cleveland Press and it was published Saturday, September the 24th, 1938. What appears to me is that, alright so let's say he was getting royalties on recordings and maybe some royalties from the publishers, his music, but it hadn't been used in a movie before so this was an opportunity for him to really make some money on "St. Louis Blues". And I suppose he did very well because as you said before they had their own publishing company. And they had another opportunity to earn some royalties from through movie re-writes to another movie that they made subsequently, also called "The Saint Louis Blues", in which Nat King Cole and Lena Horne appeared. And the old one is now called "The Best Of The Blues". But this indicates that on two occasions the "Saint Louis Blues" had an opportunity to do something with the movie rights. This is really interesting. But up until that time, you see, I was in Florence, Alabama about ten years ago when they dedicated the shrine, the W. C. Handy shrine in Florence, Alabama. It seems that previous to that,

S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC.
WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

the cabin had been standing there in a dilapidated condition, but the Housing Development had come through that area and a group of local citizens and of course with the help of the family, they decided that they were going to preserve the cabin. So it was torn down and they stored the logs around in different areas around, some in school yards, and they started out on a ten-year plan to re-structure the W. C. Handy house that he was born in, and also to set up a little W.C. Handy museum.

So I happened to be lucky enough to be down there when they dedicated the shirne. They had rebuilt the house with most of the original logs. Of course it's cement between the logs now. It's a two-room house and it's got a fire place and the old lamps they used in the early days. They have it converted to electrical fixtures, of course./ And the morning of the dedication they made a fire in the fire place and as the smoke came out of the chimney, Sharkey Bonano played "The Saint Louis Blues". And of course that day school was out and every kid that was in a band was on the streets. They had a parade. I was in one of the cars. And on every corner they was playing "The Saint Louis Blues".

S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC.
WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

And strangely enough the temperature went down to 19° that day. And some of the kids that were cheerleaders with the scanty costumes on, I think their legs were blue from the cold. And of course the people on the side lines were watching with ski masks on because it was really cold. It had gone down to 19° that day. But they had established the W. C. Handy Museum right in back of the house with the help of the W. C. Handy family. They have all of his artifacts there. It's quite a thing.. It is now a national shrine. And it's at a point where three states meet, Tennessee, Mississippi, and Alabama. So it's quite an attraction there. So something has been done.
But of course, you know, they issued a postage stamp in memory of W. C. Handy. I don't remember what year.
Daddy of the Blues, they call it.
